Senses.Explanation: To raise singly is to bring one saying, question, or Chan device forward without auxiliary explanation or divided attention. Chan records use the verb with an expressed object: a single word 'no,' the first phrase, the upward move, the command, this matter, or a hair-blowing sharp sword. They also oppose 'raising alone and handling alone' to 'dragging through water and mud,' and place 'raise directly and singly' beside the transmission outside teachings and not establishing written words. The public-interview shape remains visible when an unnamed monastic asks how Yuanwu Keqin treats people while 'today singly raising the command' and receives a blow. The Chan-specific bend is this productive teaching-seat verb: what is singled out may be a word, phrase, matter, sword, move, or command. Because those nouns are different objects of the same transitive act, they do not require separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Blood under the skin is the records' bodily image for someone who registers pain and itching, unlike unresponsive earth and wood. It is consequently used by Gulin Qingmao as a qualification for people addressed in the hall: "you people must have blood under the skin" (汝諸人須是皮下有血始得), and "if he has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood" (他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯). A garden exchange also keeps the literal body image audible: seeing a cook cut melons, Yu'an Zhiji asks the head cook, "which one has blood under the skin?" (那個皮下有血). Zen bends the bodily phrase into a recurrent test for someone who registers a touch or blow, while the records themselves ground that use in pain and itching rather than an imported psychological category.
